newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak cbank sees SKK rate mantainable in mid-term.
newsitem.headline: Slovak cbank sees SKK rate mantainable in mid-term.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia on Friday said current crown movements were in line with expectations and it believed the crown rate could be maintained over the medium term.
"We think the current rate of the Slovak crown is real and maintainable at least in the medium term," NBS Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters.
Szulenyi also said the NBS would continue adding liquidity to the market in the near future, and that the bank expected liquidity to significantly improve in coming days.
"The banking sector on Friday did not meet its minimum reserves requirements (PMR), but we expect crown liquidity to be significantly better in the next PMR period," Szulenyi said.
The next PMR period starts on Monday and will last until the end of the month.
The NBS has been battling speculative downward pressure on the crown for weeks by keeping the market illiquid.

The Slovak crown on Friday traded in a narrow range of some 10 basis points on the depreciation side of its mark/dollar basket parity. Earlier on Friday, the NBS fixed the crown at 33.488 to the dollar and at 19.367 to the mark, implying a deviation against the basket of -0.37 percent.

The NBS said it saw gradual return of foreign capital to Slovakia, estimating some $250 million has flowed into the local interbank market through its daily fixing since a slight easing of pressure on the currency a few days ago.
Szulenyi said high interbank money market rates would have a negative impact on the country's economy and that they cannot be sustained at current levels for the longer term. He did not elaborate.
Short-term money market rates continued to hover above 33 percent on Friday.
"We can see rates have started to ease in recent days and expectations are that they should keep with their gradual downtrend in the near future," Szulenyi said.
When asked what level the NBS expected rates to stabilise in the longer-term, Szulenyi said: "They should go under 20 percent, but it is hard to talk about precise figures at the moment."
